intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that ectodermal dysplasia-19, hypohidrotic/tooth/nail type (ECTD19), is caused by heterozygous mutation in the IRF6 gene (607199) on chromosome 1q32.2.

paragraphs.text: Ectodermal dysplasia-19 (ECTD19) is defined by the combination of oligodontia, hypo- or anhidrosis, hidradenitis suppurativa-like skin abscesses, poikiloderma, onychodysplasia, and bilateral hearing impairment. Natal teeth and sparse hair are irregular or variable features. Lip pits and cleft lip/palate were absent in all 5 patients known at the time of the report by Schneider et al. (2026).

paragraphs.text: Schneider et al. (2026) reported 2 unrelated teenage boys, aged 17 (P1) and 14 (P2) years. Both had drawn attention on their first day of life because of natal teeth. P1 had delayed eruption of the deciduous teeth and oligodontia, with absent mandibular incisors, canines, and permanent premolars. He also had enamel hypomineralization, dental fistulas or cysts, and an atrophic mandibular alveolar crest. P2 developed only 9 permanent teeth, and 2 molars had to be extracted because they were displaced and impacted. Both boys had anhidrosis with episodes of overheating. Sweat glands were absent in P1, and confocal laser scanning microscopy found no sweat glands on the palms of P2. Both boys had recurrent hidradenitis suppurativa-like skin abscesses, dry skin, plantar hyperkeratosis, blistering on the backs of the toes (in winter in P1), and poikiloderma. Some toenails and fingernails were dysplastic, thickened, or deformed with distal onycholysis. Both boys also had increased thick nasal mucus, dry cerumen, and bilateral sensorineural hearing impairment since infancy, treated with hearing aids. P1 tended toward allergies, with several anaphylactic reactions to milk protein among other antigens. Skin histology in P1 showed focal subcorneal clefting and basal spongiosis. Neither boy had cleft lip/palate, submucous cleft palate, lip pits, or sparse hair.

paragraphs.text: Schneider et al. (2026) also reported a 22-year-old woman (P3), born to healthy nonconsanguineous parents. She was referred for anhidrosis, dry skin, and intolerance to environmental temperatures above 22 degrees C. Examination showed diffuse xerosis, dilated follicular ostia, hidradenitis suppurativa-like skin abscesses in the groins, axillae, and intergluteal fold, pincer nails on both big toes, and poikiloderma. She had bilateral acquired sensorineural hearing loss with tympanic membrane retraction and atelectasis. Other findings were epistaxis, crusted rhinitis, insufficient salivation, bilateral superficial punctate keratitis, and a reduced tear film break-up time. After delayed tooth eruption she had 16 persisting deciduous teeth and only 2 permanent teeth. Skin biopsy showed absent sweat glands, focal subcorneal clefting, and basal spongiosis. She did not have natal teeth, and her scalp hair, eyebrows, eyelashes, breasts, and nipples were normal. She had no syndactyly and no lip or palate abnormality.

paragraphs.text: In 2 unrelated boys with ECTD19, Schneider et al. (2026) analyzed DNA from blood cells and found the same heterozygous c.653T-A transversion in exon 6 of the IRF6 gene. The change was predicted to be deleterious and results in an ile218-to-asn (I218N) substitution. It was classified as de novo because the parents' DNA showed no alteration at this position. In a 22-year-old woman with ECTD19, trio whole-genome sequencing found a de novo c.658T-C transition in IRF6, resulting in a ser220-to-pro (S220P) substitution. The variant allele frequency of 30.5% indicated mosaicism. Schneider et al. (2026) noted that these substitutions in exon 6 lie between the DNA-binding and protein-binding domains, in a region with no assigned function. AlphaFold3 modeling placed both substitutions in a short alpha-helix at the end of this region, which was predicted with higher confidence than the rest of the region.
